title: Which Banknotes Get the Best Exchange Rates for Spending Money in Thailand?

body_markdown:
Picture a Superrich counter in Bangkok. A traveler slides over three crisp 100 USD notes. The person behind him offers a fan of 5 and 10 USD notes. Both look up at the same rate board, and they are quoting from different rows.


Moreta builds a wallet for travelers who pay local QR codes across Asia and Latin America. This guide covers the cash side of the same question: what a dollar, euro or pound actually turns into at a real counter.


## Why do larger banknotes get a better exchange rate?


Money changers post tiered rates by denomination. In November 2026,


[Superrich Thailand's rate board](https://www.superrichthailand.com/exchange-rate)


paid 33.80 THB for the largest US dollar notes, and smaller denominations received progressively lower rates. Euro and British pound notes are tiered the same way.


The tiered board is the core of this whole question. It explains why the notes you pack at home matter, although the counter you pick matters more.


The usual reason is handling cost. A changer inspects, counts, stores and eventually resells every foreign note it buys. Checking a 5 USD note takes about as much work as checking a 100 USD note. Spread that fixed cost over less money and the rate gets worse.


A bakery works the same way. A full tray of bread costs less per loaf than one loaf at the counter, because the work of selling it barely changes with size.


- At Superrich in November 2026, the largest US dollar notes received 33.80 THB.


- At that rate, one 100 USD note becomes 3,380 THB.


- Smaller US dollar notes, euro notes and pound notes sit on progressively lower tiers.


## How should you convert US dollars, euros, GBP or Australian dollars at the best rate?


The tiered system means one rule covers every home currency: bring the highest-value note your bank will give you, in good condition.


Swipe for more


Home currency What to bring What to watch


US dollars 100 USD notes, recent series, unmarked Small notes like 5 USD and 10 USD sit on lower tiers


Euro 100 EUR notes or higher 50 EUR and smaller notes sit on a lower tier


GBP 50 GBP notes 20 GBP and smaller notes sit on a lower tier


Australian dollar Clean, undamaged notes Check the posted rate before you exchange


Changers inspect notes closely. Torn, written-on or visibly worn notes are the ones most likely to be turned away. Ask your home bank for clean notes when you order currency.


## Where is the best money changer?


The best counter is the one with a public rate board that you have checked against at least one competitor. Travel guides regularly single out specific exchange offices for this reason.


- **Superrich exchange rate:**


This is the reference point most travelers use. Two separate companies trade under the Superrich name, so compare their boards rather than assuming they match.


- **Vasu Exchange:**


This Sukhumvit changer is a common alternative to compare against Superrich.


- **The airport:**


Change only enough at the airport to cover your train or taxi into the city.


- **City currency exchange:**


Booths cluster around Rajdamri, where Superrich has its headquarters, and along Sukhumvit. Read the posted rates before you commit.


**How to exchange money at a counter:**


1. Bring your passport. Licensed changers ask for it.


2. Read the board for your currency and your note size.


3. Hand over your notes and say the total you expect in local currency.


4. Count the local currency at the window before you step away.


## Are ATM fees worse than exchanging cash?


For most visitors, yes, because of the fee structure rather than the exchange rate. Thai bank ATMs charge a flat fee on every foreign-card withdrawal, and your home bank may add its own charges on top.


A flat fee rewards fewer, larger withdrawals. Five small withdrawals cost five times the fee of one larger one.


The bigger trap is dynamic currency conversion (DCC). The ATM or card terminal offers to charge you in your home currency. If you accept, the machine operator sets the conversion rate instead of your card network. Decline it every time and choose local currency.


## Which notes should you carry once you have exchanged?


The logic flips after the exchange. You wanted big foreign notes going in, and you want small local notes coming out.


Every standard denomination is legal tender. In practice, small vendors routinely refuse the largest notes because they have no change.


Picture a coconut ice cream seller at a weekend market. She looks at your largest note, then at her biscuit tin of smaller bills, and shakes her head.


- **Break big notes at chains.**


A 7-Eleven counter can break a 1,000 baht note.


- **Keep a working stack.**


Carry 100 and 20 baht notes for street food and motorbike taxis.


- **Hold coins for small costs.**


Keep small coins for public toilets and donation boxes.


## What should you set up before you fly?


- Order clean, high-value notes from your home bank one to two weeks before departure.


- Call your card issuer about foreign ATM fees, and plan fewer, larger withdrawals as a backup.


- If you are visiting multiple countries, research the local payment networks for each one. Malaysia runs on[DuitNow QR](https://moretapay.com/networks/duitnow) and Cambodia on[KHQR](https://moretapay.com/networks/khqr) , where US dollars and local currency circulate side by side.


For those stops, Moreta Pay follows the same steps in each country:


1. Top up in your own currency from your home bank or card.


2. Scan the merchant's local QR code.


3. Check the merchant name, amount and exact FX rate before you slide to confirm.


4. The merchant is paid instantly in local currency.


Moreta reports a single 1.5% payment fee, shown on screen before you confirm.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is it cheaper to exchange money at home or abroad?


It is usually cheaper to exchange large notes at a city money changer, where rates are posted and easy to compare.


### Do money changers accept damaged notes?


Torn, marked or heavily worn notes are often refused. Bring clean notes.


### How much does an ATM withdrawal cost?


Thai bank ATMs charge a flat operator fee on each foreign-card withdrawal, and your home bank's fees come on top.


### Can I spend US dollars directly?


Plan to pay in local currency. Local currency is the official tender, and everyday merchants price in it.


### Will street vendors accept the largest notes?


They often will not. Break it at a convenience store first.


### Do I need a passport to exchange money?


Yes. Licensed changers ask for it.
